_about: Landmark hints for the world satellite warm-up: [hint shown after the tap, landmark longitude, landmark latitude, landmark label]. Each hint points at something you can actually see on the satellite map (a river, delta, lake, bay, ridge, volcano, peninsula, moorland or island), never at a border, ruin or name you can't see from space. A hint never names another warm-up city from the same state, so it can't give the next one away. Run `node genpinll.mjs` to turn these into the game's PIN_HINTS.

New Orleans: Squeezed between round, dark Lake Pontchartrain and a big bend of the Mississippi, about 75 miles upriver from where the river's bird's-foot delta pokes out into the Gulf.
Baton Rouge: On the winding Mississippi, about 50 miles west of the round, dark Lake Pontchartrain.
Shreveport: Where the Red River's winding green valley crosses Louisiana's northwest corner, about 15 miles east of swampy Caddo Lake.
Lafayette: Just west of the Atchafalaya Basin, the dark green strip of swamp forest that runs straight down to the Gulf.
Austin: On the Colorado River right where the chain of dark, snaking Hill Country reservoirs (like Lake Travis) ends and the flat farmland begins.
Houston: A huge gray sprawl about 25 miles inland from Galveston Bay, the big notched bay behind a long, thin barrier island.
El Paso: Where the Rio Grande's thin green ribbon of farms squeezes past the southern tip of the Franklin Mountains, a lone dark ridge in the desert.
Dallas: A huge gray sprawl on the flat north Texas prairie, ringed by reservoirs; Lewisville Lake sits just to the northwest.
San Antonio: At the southern edge of the green, rumpled Hill Country, where it drops onto the flat brown south Texas plains, about 30 miles southwest of Canyon Lake.
Nashville: On a twisting loop of the Cumberland River, just west of the dark, branching reservoirs of Percy Priest and Old Hickory lakes.
Memphis: On the east bank of the Mississippi, where the river's wide band of green floodplain and crescent-shaped oxbow lakes runs past the bluffs.
Knoxville: On the Tennessee River among east Tennessee's long, striped ridges, about 30 miles northwest of the dark green wall of the Great Smoky Mountains.
Chattanooga: Where the Tennessee River makes tight bends through the long, striped ridges, at the foot of Lookout Mountain.
Los Angeles: A giant gray sprawl filling the basin between the San Gabriel Mountains and Santa Monica Bay, where the coast turns east.
San Francisco: On the big bay halfway up California's coast, at the tip of the peninsula between the bay and the Pacific.
Sacramento: In the flat green-and-tan Central Valley, just north of the Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta, a maze of islands and channels.
San Diego: Around a hooked bay sheltered by the long Point Loma peninsula, in the very bottom-left corner of the state.
New York City: At the state's southern tip, where the Hudson River meets the Atlantic, right beside Long Island.
Albany: On the Hudson, just below where the Mohawk River comes in from the west through its long valley, with the dark green Adirondacks rising to the north.
Buffalo: At the eastern tip of Lake Erie, where the Niagara River runs north to Lake Ontario.
Syracuse: Between Lake Ontario and the long, thin, parallel Finger Lakes that look like claw scratches from space.
Honolulu: On the south shore of Oʻahu, between the branching inlets of Pearl Harbor and the round crater of Diamond Head.
Hilo: On a curved bay on the Big Island's wet, green east side, below the long slopes of Mauna Kea.
Lahaina: On the west coast of Maui, looking across the channel at the island of Lānaʻi.
Kailua-Kona: On the Big Island's dry west coast, where black lava flows from Hualālai volcano run down to the sea.

London: A huge gray sprawl on the Thames, about 50 miles upriver from where it widens into its funnel-shaped estuary.
Birmingham: A big gray sprawl right in the middle of England, about 45 miles south of the Peak District's dark moorland.
Manchester: A big gray sprawl at the western foot of the Pennines, the dark brown moorland spine running up northern England.
Liverpool: At the mouth of the River Mersey, the wide estuary opening into the Irish Sea beside the stubby Wirral peninsula.
Leeds: In Yorkshire, on the east side of the Pennines, just southeast of the Yorkshire Dales.
Newcastle: In the northeast, on the River Tyne just before it reaches the North Sea, about 60 miles south of Scotland.
Bristol: In the southwest, where the Severn estuary opens into the Bristol Channel, with Wales across the water.
Sheffield: In South Yorkshire, on the eastern edge of the Peak District hills.
Nottingham: On the River Trent in flat farmland, about 20 miles east of the Peak District's dark hills.
Plymouth: On the south coast at a branching inlet, just south of the big brown patch of Dartmoor's moorland.
Norwich: In the round bulge of East Anglia, just west of the Norfolk Broads, a maze of small lakes and rivers near the coast.
York: In the flat green Vale of York, about 25 miles southwest of the dark heather of the North York Moors.
Oxford: On the upper Thames, at the eastern edge of the Cotswold hills.
Cambridge: At the southern edge of the Fens, the dead-flat, ruler-straight fields that run up to the square bay of the Wash.
Brighton: On the south coast at the foot of the South Downs, a long bare chalk ridge running east to west.
Southampton: At the head of a long, straight inlet, Southampton Water, just north of the diamond-shaped Isle of Wight.
Dover: At England's southeast tip, the closest point to France, by the White Cliffs.
Carlisle: At the head of the Solway Firth, the wide tidal estuary between England and Scotland, just north of the Lake District's mountains.
Canterbury: In Kent, England's southeast corner, about 10 miles south of the mouth of the Thames Estuary.
Edinburgh: On the south shore of the Firth of Forth, the big inlet on Scotland's east coast.
Glasgow: On the River Clyde in the west, just inland from where it opens into the Firth of Clyde.
Aberdeen: On the northeast coast at the mouth of the River Dee, about 60 miles east of the dark, often snowy Cairngorm mountains.
Dundee: On the north shore of the Firth of Tay, on the east coast.
Inverness: Where the long, dead-straight dark line of Loch Ness and the Great Glen meets the Moray Firth.
Stirling: At Scotland's narrow waist, where the River Forth widens into the Firth of Forth.
Perth: On the River Tay at the edge of the Highlands, a few miles upriver from the Firth of Tay.
Fort William: At the southwest end of the Great Glen, beneath Ben Nevis, Britain's highest mountain.
St Andrews: On the east coast of Fife, the peninsula between the Firth of Forth and the Firth of Tay.
Oban: On the west coast, looking out at the Isle of Mull, the 'gateway to the Isles'.
Kirkwall: On Orkney, the islands just across the Pentland Firth from mainland Scotland's northern tip.
Lerwick: On Shetland, the northernmost islands, more than 100 miles north of the mainland, past Orkney.
Cardiff: On the south coast, on the Bristol Channel, with England across the water.
Swansea: On the south coast, on a wide bay at the base of the Gower Peninsula.
Newport: In the southeast corner, by the mouth of the Severn, where the bridges cross into England.
Wrexham: Where the green Welsh hills drop onto the flat Cheshire plain, about 20 miles south of the Dee estuary's wide, sandy mouth.
Bangor: On the north coast at the Menai Strait, looking across to the island of Anglesey.
Aberystwyth: Halfway down the long west coast, in the middle of Cardigan Bay.
Holyhead: On Holy Island off Anglesey's west tip, the ferry port for Ireland.
St Davids: At the very tip of the southwest peninsula, Pembrokeshire, beside St Brides Bay.
Caernarfon: On the Menai Strait across from Anglesey, at the foot of Snowdon, Wales's highest peak.
Llandudno: On the north coast between the Great Orme and Little Orme headlands, on Liverpool Bay.
Brecon: In the middle of south Wales, at the foot of the Brecon Beacons mountains.
Carmarthen: In the southwest, on the River Tywi, just inland from Carmarthen Bay.
Belfast: At the head of Belfast Lough, the inlet on the east coast that faces Scotland.
Derry: In the northwest, on the River Foyle just before it widens into Lough Foyle, right by the border with the Republic.
Armagh: In the south, about 10 miles south of Lough Neagh, the biggest lake in the British Isles.
Newry: At the head of Carlingford Lough, the narrow sea inlet just west of the dark Mourne Mountains.
Enniskillen: In the southwest, on the island between Upper and Lower Lough Erne.
Omagh: In the west, in County Tyrone, just south of the Sperrin Mountains.
Coleraine: A few miles inland from the north coast on the River Bann, east of Lough Foyle.
Ballymena: In County Antrim, about 10 miles north of Lough Neagh.
Bushmills: On the north coast by the Giant's Causeway, facing Rathlin Island.
Lisburn: About 10 miles east of Lough Neagh's southeast shore, on the River Lagan.
Downpatrick: Near the east coast, at the southern end of Strangford Lough, where St Patrick is said to be buried.
Dublin: Halfway down the east coast on Dublin Bay, just north of the dark Wicklow Mountains.
Cork: On the south coast, at the head of Cork Harbour, one of the world's biggest natural harbors.
Galway: On the west coast at the head of Galway Bay, with the Aran Islands at the bay's mouth.
Limerick: In the southwest, where the River Shannon widens into its long estuary.
Waterford: On the southeast coast, on the River Suir just above Waterford Harbour.
Kilkenny: Inland in the southeast, on the River Nore, about 30 miles north of Waterford Harbour.
Sligo: On the northwest coast, on Sligo Bay, beneath flat-topped Benbulben mountain.
Killarney: In the far southwest, beside the Lakes of Killarney and Carrauntoohil, Ireland's highest mountain.
Athlone: Right in the middle of Ireland, where the River Shannon leaves Lough Ree.
Donegal: In the northwest, at the head of Donegal Bay.
Wexford: In the southeast corner, at the mouth of the River Slaney, facing St George's Channel and Wales.
Westport: On the west coast at Clew Bay, beneath the holy mountain Croagh Patrick.
Dingle: Out on the Dingle Peninsula, the long finger of land reaching into the Atlantic in the southwest.

Mexico City: A vast gray sprawl filling a high valley, about 40 miles northwest of the snowy volcano Popocatépetl.
Puebla: Just east of the two big volcanoes, Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl.
Toluca: In its own high valley, just northeast of the Nevado de Toluca volcano.
Cuernavaca: About 40 miles west of Popocatépetl, where the land drops into warmer valleys: the 'city of eternal spring'.
Querétaro: On the central plateau, just southwest of the rugged Sierra Gorda mountains.
Pachuca: At the foot of the forested Sierra de Pachuca, on the edge of the dry, tan Mezquital valley.
Tlaxcala: Just west of La Malinche volcano, in Mexico's smallest state.
Morelia: About 20 miles south of Lake Cuitzeo, a big, shallow, muddy-colored lake.
Taxco: Up in the silver-mining mountains of northern Guerrero, about 40 miles south of the Nevado de Toluca volcano.
Acapulco: On the Pacific coast, almost straight south of the capital, wrapped around a horseshoe-shaped bay.
Veracruz: On the Gulf of Mexico coast, about 75 miles east of Pico de Orizaba, Mexico's highest peak.
Xalapa: In the misty hills just east of the Cofre de Perote volcano, halfway down to the Gulf coast.
Guanajuato: In the rumpled Sierra de Guanajuato hills, just above the Bajío, a flat patchwork of green farm fields.
Mérida: In the flat, green-brown northwest of the Yucatán, about 20 miles inland from the Gulf coast's thin lagoons.
Cancún: At the peninsula's northeast corner, beside a thin sandbar shaped like a 7, across from the long, skinny Isla Mujeres.
Campeche: On the west side of the peninsula, facing the Bay of Campeche.
Chetumal: At the head of a big sheltered bay on the Caribbean coast, behind a long peninsula, near the peninsula's southern end.
Valladolid: In the middle of the flat, jungle-covered north of the peninsula, about 60 miles south of the pink Ría Lagartos lagoons.
Playa del Carmen: On the Caribbean coast's straight line of white beaches, about 35 miles south of the peninsula's northeast corner.
Tulum: On the Caribbean coast, at the north edge of Sian Ka'an, a huge reserve of lagoons and wetlands.
Progreso: On the north coast of the peninsula, where the shallow turquoise Gulf of Mexico meets a strip of thin lagoons.
Izamal: In the flat north-central Yucatán, about 28 miles inland from the Gulf coast's thin lagoons.
Ciudad del Carmen: On a long island between the Gulf and the Laguna de Términos, at the southwest base of the peninsula.
Cozumel: On Mexico's biggest Caribbean island, just off the east coast of the peninsula.
Bacalar: On a long, thin, turquoise lagoon running parallel to the Caribbean coast, near the peninsula's southern end.
Tizimín: In the northeast, about 30 miles inland from the Ría Lagartos flamingo lagoon.
Guadalajara: About 25 miles north of Lake Chapala, Mexico's biggest lake.
Puerto Vallarta: On the Pacific at the head of the Bay of Banderas, one of the biggest bays in Mexico.
Tequila: At the foot of the Tequila volcano, surrounded by blue agave fields.
Colima: About 20 miles south of the Colima volcano, one of Mexico's most active.
Manzanillo: On the Pacific between two round bays, at the north end of the long Cuyutlán lagoon that runs down the coast.
Tepic: In Nayarit, beside the Sangangüey volcano, about 30 miles inland from the Pacific.
Aguascalientes: On the high, dry, tan central plateau, about 120 miles north-northeast of big blue Lake Chapala.
Zacatecas: In the high, dry north-central country, east of the Sierra Madre Occidental mountains.
León: In the Bajío highlands, about 100 miles northeast of Lake Chapala.
Lagos de Moreno: On the high, dry, tan plateau, about 100 miles northeast of big blue Lake Chapala.
Ciudad Guzmán: On the shore of Lake Zapotlán, just northeast of the Colima volcano.
Ajijic: On the north shore of Lake Chapala.
Havana: On the north coast of long, thin Cuba's western end, about 100 miles south of the curving chain of the Florida Keys.
Santiago de Cuba: On the southeast coast, below the Sierra Maestra and Pico Turquino, Cuba's highest peak.
Camagüey: Inland in the middle of the long eastern half, about 50 miles south of Cayo Romano, one of Cuba's biggest offshore cays.
Holguín: On the plains in the northeast, about 30 miles inland from the north coast's ragged, notched bays, like Bariay Bay.
Santa Clara: In the center of the island, just north of the Escambray Mountains.
Cienfuegos: On a big bay on the south coast, about 45 miles east of the Bay of Pigs.
Trinidad: On the south coast, at the foot of the Escambray Mountains.
Matanzas: On a deep bay on the north coast, facing the Straits of Florida.
Varadero: On the long, thin Hicacos Peninsula on the north coast, facing the Straits of Florida.
Pinar del Río: In the far west, just south of the dark green Sierra de los Órganos hills.
Guantánamo: Near the island's southeast tip, just inland from Guantánamo Bay.
Baracoa: On the north coast of the far eastern tip, near the Windward Passage to Haiti.
Bayamo: In the east, on the plains north of the Sierra Maestra and Pico Turquino.
Kingston: On the southeast coast, at a big natural harbor below the Blue Mountains.
Montego Bay: On the northwest coast, at a big curved bay facing the open Caribbean.
Ocho Rios: In the middle of the north coast, where green hills drop straight into the sea, about 40 miles northwest of the dark Blue Mountains.
Negril: At the island's far western tip, along Seven Mile Beach.
Port Antonio: On the northeast coast, on the far side of the Blue Mountains.
Spanish Town: On the southern plains on the Rio Cobre, inland from Portland Bight: the old Spanish capital.
Mandeville: High in the hilly center-west, just east of the Santa Cruz Mountains.
May Pen: On the southern plains on the Rio Minho, just inland from Portland Bight.
Falmouth: On the north coast at the mouth of the Martha Brae River, beside a small, shallow lagoon.
Port Royal: At the end of the long Palisadoes sandspit on the southeast coast, the old pirate capital.
Black River: On the southwest coast at the mouth of the Black River, next to the Great Morass wetland.
Morant Bay: Near the southeast tip, south of the Blue Mountains.
San Juan: On the north coast near the east end, around a big sheltered bay facing the Atlantic.
Ponce: In the middle of the south coast, facing the Caribbean, below the green Cordillera Central mountains.
Mayagüez: On the west coast, facing the Mona Passage toward the Dominican Republic.
Arecibo: On the north coast where the Río Grande de Arecibo comes out of the green, pitted karst hills.
Caguas: In a valley in the east-central interior, about 20 miles southwest of the El Yunque rainforest.
Bayamón: On the north coast plain, just inland from the Atlantic, east of the island's middle.
Fajardo: At the island's northeast corner, the ferry port for the island of Culebra.
Aguadilla: At the island's northwest corner, where the Atlantic meets the Mona Passage.
Humacao: On the east coast, south of the El Yunque rainforest.
Guayama: On the southeast coast, below the Sierra de Cayey mountains.
Isabela: On the northwest coast's surf beaches, facing the Atlantic.
Cabo Rojo: In the far southwest corner, by the lighthouse on the red cliffs at the Mona Passage.
Vieques: An island off Puerto Rico's east coast, just south of Culebra.
